newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE - Mexico's recovery leaves many behind.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Mexico's recovery leaves many behind.

text.p: Laura Fernandez and her father wait patiently for a lawyer in the twilight of a dilapidated concrete office in Mexico City.

She is 42, single, and earns 2,000 pesos ($253) a month as a secretary. Dressed smartly for work, she clutches a letter from the major Mexican bank Banamex demanding payment of a 57,000 peso ($7,215) credit card bill and threatening legal action.

"We can't pay in one go what they are asking," she tells the lawyer at the Mexican debtors' group El Barzon (the yoke), one of the country's biggest protest groups which represents more than a million bank debtors nationwide.

Fernandez has put on a brave face but has come here in fear, because a bill of 6,000 pesos ($760), manageable more than two years ago, became a monster when interest rates soared in the wake of the December 1994 peso crash.
She says she has been intimidated by 3.00 a.m. telephone threats, though Banamex denies it allows calls after 9.30 at night through the debt collectors it contracts.
Fernandez is just one of Banamex's current 200,000 credit card debtors, who, together with thousands more Mexico-wide, are still struggling to pay for Mexico's financial crisis.

The amount of consumer debt, including credit card and durable good loans, still owed to banks in December 1996 totalled eight billion pesos ($1.01 billion), according to Rogelio Ramirez, director of economic advisors Ecanal.
Government subsidies via lower interest rates helped bring that down from 13 billion pesos ($1.64 billion) when the crisis broke in December 1994.

But mortgage debt over the same period has soared -- to 205 billion pesos ($26 billion) from 103 billion ($13 billion) Ramirez says -- because housing loans restructured after the crisis were indexed to consumer price inflation and therefore continued to grow.

"I calculate that about one million households are currently trapped in these mortgage loans," he said. "Families have been repaying their credit card and consumer loans but housing loans are...not being repaid."
The repercussions of the crisis are still being felt at every tourist spot and every traffic light across the city, where more street vendors vie for trade than ever.
Though reliable data is unavailable, armed street crime has increased as levels of desperation rise.
JULY ELECTIONS
Jose Luis Gomez Castaneda, a lawyer for El Barzon which was set up to defend citizens' rights and fight the banks through the courts, says the number of cases is still growing.
"The numbers are just ballooning," he says. "We have 300 to 350 court cases at the moment and the number will double in the next two months."
Ramirez agreed that housing repossessions, on hold during the run-up to mid-term elections scheduled for July, would rise steeply after the poll.
The debt overhang is one of the reasons why Mexico's gradual recovery from the 1994-5 crisis has so far failed to generate any feel-good factor among ordinary people ahead of the July 6 vote.

Government predictions this week of five percent growth and a million new jobs a year by 2000 sound hollow to thousands of households still struggling to eliminate domestic debt and recover their former standard of living.
Clients of El Barzon are not alone in wondering why they are not feeling the much-trumpeted economic rebound.
A LACKLUSTRE FIRST QUARTER

Mexico's first quarter GDP growth came at an unspectacular 5.1 percent after 7.6 percent in the fourth quarter last year, while retail sales for the first three months showed a discouraging 3.5 percent slump.
Then came a rise in April unemployment and a four percent plunge in supermarket sales, dashing hopes that a broad-based revival in domestic consumption might finally have begun to materialise.

Seasonally adjusted, the growth figures looked even less good -- just 3.9 percent for the fourth quarter of 1996 and 0.9 percent in the first quarter of this year, according to Alfredo Thorne, an economist at JP Morgan here.

"The depressed level of activity created by the deep 1995 recession facilitated very high year-on-year growth rates during 1996. But these are seen to be illusory once the data are restated in seasonally adjusted terms," he said.
Other analysts say the picture is not that bleak.
A sharp decline in Mexico's April trade surplus, though it jangled the nerves of currency traders, showed a surprise increase in imports, suggesting some life in the domestic market after all.
"It does suggest we may be seeing signs of a revival," said Denis Parisien, vice president for Latin American Research at Bankers Trust in New York.
AN UPTURN IN CONSUMPTION
Economists like Parisien and Thorne are pinning their hopes on a second-half upturn in domestic consumption to breathe life into the country's still fragile economy.

The Mexican Bankers Association said some 430,000 people have benefited from government schemes to restructure mortgages, 480,000 from others rescheduling consumer loans and 504,000 from programmes restructuring company debt.
"The numbers (of those needing help) have diminished considerably because of the 1995 and 1996 restructuring schemes," said a spokesman for the association.

Though the total number of debtors may be diminishing, domestic demand remains stubbornly weak and analysts say this is because earnings are still going into paying back borrowings rather than into fresh spending.

Hector Chavez, chief economist for Mexico at Banco Santander here, said sub-inflation increases in the minimum wage and real declines in its purchasing power had played a big part in keeping consumption low.
Mexico City's current minimum wage of 26.4 pesos ($3.34) a day has risen 73 percent since 1994 against a 109 percent climb in inflation, he said.
The cost of a basic basket of necessary consumer goods has risen about 110 percent.
"People on low incomes have been hit hardest -- inflation on that basket of goods has been higher," Chavez said.
But analysts here expect real wages to finally start to recover in the second half of this year, bringing a upturn in consumption in its train.

"When inflation spikes from 8.0 percent to 50 percent a year with such a shock, and real incomes decline to such a degree, it takes a long time to unwind from that kind of strain," said Bankers Trust's Parisien, comparing 1994 and 1995 inflation levels.
"It's been a truly brutal transformation for people to go through and that sort of situation doesn't get fixed overnight."
